How to use this book

This is a git tutorial you type your way through. Each chapter is a scenario. Every step says what you are about to do, then gives the command as its own line, then explains what git actually did, in terms of the three places every command touches: the working tree (the files on disk), the index or staging area (the snapshot you are preparing), and the repository (the committed history in .git).

Commits form a graph: each one points at a snapshot and at its parents. Branches and tags are just names pointing at commits, and HEAD names the commit you are standing on. Keep that picture in mind and every command becomes obvious.

At the end of each chapter there is a drill: the chapter's commands again, in order, without explanations. Type the drill until your fingers know it. Angle brackets mark values you would replace in real life; here, type them as written.
Chapter 1. Set up your identity
Before the first commit, git needs to know who you are and how you like to work. You will do this once per machine. Open a terminal.
Tell git your name; it goes into every commit you make.
git config --global user.name "Ganindu Nanayakkara"

Global means the value is stored in ~/.gitconfig and applies to every repository on this machine. The same option without --global writes to .git/config of the current repository, which overrides the global value.
Tell git your e-mail; hosting services match it to your account.
git config --global user.email ganindu@example.com
Use an address the service knows, or the noreply address it gives you, otherwise your commits are not credited to you.
Make new repositories start on main.
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
Only git init looks at this; existing repositories keep whatever branch they have.
Make pull replay your commits on top of the fetched ones instead of merging.
git config --global pull.rebase true
Your history stays linear. Replayed commits get new hashes, which is fine for commits you have not pushed yet.
Give yourself a readable history command.
git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --decorate --all"
Aliases live in the config and expand before git runs, so git lg now draws every branch as a compact graph.
Check what you set and where each value came from.
git config --list --show-origin
Every effective setting with the file it lives in: system, global or local. When two files disagree, the more local one wins.

Drill. From memory, in order, type: git config --global user.name "Your Name", git config --global user.email you@example.com, git config --global init.defaultBranch main, git config --global pull.rebase true, git config --list --show-origin
Chapter 2. Your first repository
You will create a throwaway project, make it a repository and record the first snapshot. Nothing here touches any other repository on your machine.
Make a directory for the experiment and go into it.
mkdir git-drill && cd git-drill
Plain shell; git is not involved yet.
Turn the directory into a repository.
git init
Git creates a hidden .git folder holding the object database, the refs and the config. The files in the directory are untracked until you add them.
Create a file to track.
echo "# git drill" > README.md
Still just the shell writing a file into the working tree.
Ask git what it sees.
git status
It reports an untracked file. Untracked means git knows nothing about it; it is neither in the index nor in any commit.
Stage the file.
git add README.md
The current content of the file is copied into the index. The next commit will contain exactly this content, even if you edit the file again before committing.
Record the snapshot.
git commit -m "Add README"
Git writes the index as a tree, wraps it in a commit object whose parent is empty because this is the first one, and points the branch main at it. HEAD points at main, so HEAD now means this commit.
Look at what you made.
git log --oneline
One line: an abbreviated hash and the subject. The hash is the name of the commit; it is computed from the content, so the same commit has the same name everywhere.
Drill. From memory, in order, type: mkdir git-drill && cd git-drill, git init, echo "# git drill" > README.md, git status, git add README.md, git commit -m "Add README", git log --oneline
Chapter 3. The everyday loop
Most of git is status, add, commit, repeated. This chapter makes the loop automatic and shows the shortcuts and the one dangerous one.
Change the file and add a second one.
echo "notes" >> README.md && echo "print('hi')" > hello.py
Now the working tree differs from the index in two ways: one tracked file is modified, one new file is untracked.
Read the short status.
git status --short
Two columns of letters per file: left is the index, right is the working tree. M means modified, A added, D deleted, ?? untracked. Once you read it fluently it is all you need.
See exactly what changed but is not staged.
git diff
Working tree against index. The new file does not appear here because git diff only shows tracked files.
Stage only part of a change.
git add -p
Git walks through each hunk and asks y or n. This is how one messy working tree becomes several clean commits: stage the hunks that belong together, commit, repeat.
Stage everything at once when it all belongs together.
git add -A
Modifications, new files and deletions across the whole working tree go into the index. Look at git status first so a stray file does not sneak in.
Check what the commit will contain.
git diff --staged
Index against HEAD: exactly the next commit. Reading this before every commit is the cheapest code review you will ever get.
Commit with the editor so you can write a real message.
git commit
First line is the subject, keep it under about fifty characters; blank line; then the reasoning in the body. Lines starting with # are comments and are dropped.
Commit all modified tracked files in one go.
git commit -am "Explain the drill"
The -a stages every modified tracked file first. It does not pick up new untracked files; for those you still need git add.
Fix the last commit instead of making a new one.
git commit --amend --no-edit
Git replaces the last commit with a new one made from the current index, keeping the message. The old commit leaves the branch, so never amend a commit that anyone else already has.
Drill. From memory, in order, type: git status --short, git diff, git add -p, git add -A, git diff --staged, git commit -m "message", git commit --amend --no-edit
Chapter 4. Reading history
A repository is worthless if you cannot ask it questions. You will learn to look at what happened, when, and why.
Show the whole history compactly.
git log --oneline
Newest first. Add -n 10 to see only the last ten.
Draw the graph of every branch.
git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate
ASCII art of the commit graph with branch and tag names next to the commits they point at. This is the picture to look at after every merge or rebase until it is intuitive.
Follow one file.
git log -p -- README.md
Only commits that touched the file, each with its diff. The double dash says: what follows is a path, not a branch.
Filter by author and date.
git log --author=ganindu --since="2 weeks ago"
Dates are forgiving: yesterday, last month, 2024-01-01 all work.
Find when a word appeared or vanished.
git log -S "hello" --oneline
The pickaxe finds commits where the number of occurrences of the string changed. This is how you discover when a function was introduced or deleted.
Inspect one commit in full.
git show HEAD~1
Metadata, message and diff. HEAD~1 is one commit back along the first parent; HEAD^ means the same; HEAD~3 is three back.
See who last touched each line.
git blame -L 1,5 README.md
Lines 1 to 5 annotated with commit and author. Follow up with git show on the hash to read why.
Drill. From memory, in order, type: git log --oneline, git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate, git log -p -- README.md, git log -S "hello" --oneline, git show HEAD~1, git blame -L 1,5 README.md
Chapter 5. Branches
You will start a piece of work on its own branch, switch back and forth, and clean up afterwards. A branch is a file containing a commit hash; creating one costs nothing.
Create a branch and move onto it.
git switch -c feature/greeting
switch is the modern command for moving between branches; checkout -b does the same. HEAD now points at the new branch, which points at the same commit main does.
Make a change and commit it on the branch.
echo "print('hello, world')" > hello.py && git commit -am "Greet the world"
The branch moves forward to the new commit; main stays where it was. The two branches have diverged by one commit.
List branches.
git branch
The star marks the current branch. Add -a to also see remote-tracking branches like origin/main, which record where the remote's branches were at your last fetch.
Go back to main.
git switch main
HEAD moves, and the working tree is rewritten to match main, so hello.py is the old version again. Git refuses to switch if it would overwrite uncommitted changes; commit or stash first.
Rename a branch.
git branch -m feature/greeting feature/hello
Only the local name changes. A remote copy keeps the old name until you push the new one and delete the old.
Delete a branch you no longer need.
git branch -d feature/hello
With lower-case -d git refuses unless the commits are reachable from elsewhere, so nothing is lost. Upper-case -D forces it. Do not run this yet; you need the branch in the next chapter.
Drill. From memory, in order, type: git switch -c feature/x, git commit -am "message", git branch, git switch main, git branch -m old new, git branch -d name
Chapter 6. Merging and rebasing
Now bring the branch's work back into main, the two ways it can be done, and learn to get out of trouble.
Merge the feature into main with a fast-forward.
git merge feature/hello
Because main has not moved since the branch was created, git simply moves main forward to the branch's commit. No merge commit is needed.
Force a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible.
git merge --no-ff feature/hello
A merge commit has two parents and shows that the feature lived on its own branch. Many teams prefer this for readability of the graph.
Escape a merge that hit conflicts.
git merge --abort
Everything goes back to the state before you started the merge. There is no shame in it; resolve the conflicts later with a clearer head.
Replay a branch on top of an updated main.
git rebase main
Git removes your branch's commits, fast-forwards the branch to main and replays the commits one by one, so the history is a straight line as if you had started from today's main.
Tidy the last few commits before sharing them.
git rebase -i HEAD~3
An editor lists the commits and you reorder, squash, reword, edit or drop. Fix typo commits become part of the change they fixed.
Carry on after fixing a conflict during a rebase.
git rebase --continue
Stage the resolved files with git add first. git rebase --abort gives up and restores the branch as it was.
Bring one commit from elsewhere onto this branch.
git cherry-pick <hash>
Applies that commit's changes as a new commit here. Useful for moving a single fix to a release branch without merging everything else.
Let git remember how you resolved conflicts.
git config --global rerere.enabled true
Reuse recorded resolution: the same conflict is resolved automatically the next time it appears, which long-lived branches and repeated rebases provoke constantly.
Drill. From memory, in order, type: git merge feature/x, git merge --no-ff feature/x, git merge --abort, git rebase main, git rebase -i HEAD~3, git rebase --continue, git cherry-pick <hash>
Chapter 7. Working with a remote
Until now everything lived on your disk. You will connect the repository to a server, publish a branch, and keep in step with others.
Clone an existing project to see the other direction.
git clone https://github.com/karpathy/micrograd.git
All commits, branches and tags come down, a remote named origin is set up pointing at the URL, and the default branch is checked out.
Register a second remote for the original project of a fork.
git remote add upstream https://github.com/aradzie/keybr.com.git
origin is your copy, upstream is the source. You fetch from upstream to keep up and push to origin.
See where pushes and fetches go.
git remote -v
Each remote with its fetch and push URL.
Download what is new without touching your branches.
git fetch --all --prune

Remote-tracking branches like origin/main are updated, remote-tracking branches for deleted remote branches are removed, and nothing in your working tree or your own branches changes. Fetch is always safe.
Bring your branch up to date.
git pull --rebase
Fetch, then replay your unpushed commits on top of the fetched ones. Without --rebase and without the pull.rebase setting, pull merges instead.
Publish a new branch and set up tracking.
git push -u origin feature/hello
Later pushes and pulls on this branch need no arguments, and git status can say ahead by two, behind by one.
Push after you have rewritten history with a rebase.
git push --force-with-lease
Overwrites the remote branch with yours, but only if the remote is still where you last saw it. Plain --force skips that check and can destroy someone else's commits; never use it on a shared branch.
Delete a branch on the remote.
git push origin --delete feature/hello
Your local branch is untouched; delete it separately with git branch -d.
Push your tags, which plain push leaves behind.
git push --tags
Push a single tag with git push origin v1.2.0.
Drill. From memory, in order, type: git fetch --all --prune, git pull --rebase, git push -u origin feature/x, git push --force-with-lease, git push origin --delete feature/x, git push --tags
Chapter 8. Undoing things
Everyone breaks something. This chapter is the set of moves that put it right, from the gentle to the drastic, and the one that brings back what looked lost.
Throw away unstaged edits to one file.
git restore hello.py
The file is rewritten from the index. Destructive and immediate; be sure.
Unstage a file you added too early.
git restore --staged hello.py
The index goes back to HEAD for that file; the working tree keeps your edits. This is the safe undo for an over-eager git add.
Undo the last commit but keep its changes staged.
git reset --soft HEAD~1
The branch moves back one commit; index and working tree stay as they were. Recommit with a better message or split it into two.
Undo the last commit and unstage its changes.
git reset HEAD~1
Mixed mode, the default: branch and index move back, the working tree is left alone, so your edits are still on disk.
Undo the last commit and discard its changes.
git reset --hard HEAD~1
Branch, index and working tree all move back. The changes vanish from disk. The old commit stays in the reflog for a while; that is your only way back.
Undo a commit that has already been pushed.
git revert <hash>
A new commit applies the inverse of the old one. Nothing is rewritten, so it is safe on shared branches; this is the correct undo once others have pulled.
Find what you thought you lost.
git reflog
Every place HEAD has pointed recently: commits, switches, resets, rebases. The hash is almost certainly here; git switch -c rescue <hash> brings it back as a branch.
Put work aside to switch branches with a clean tree.
git stash push -m "wip: greeting"
Working tree and index are saved on a stack and reset to HEAD. Name the stash; three unnamed stashes are a puzzle.
Take the work back.
git stash pop
Reapplies the most recent stash and drops it from the stack if it applied cleanly. apply reapplies without dropping; drop discards one.
Remove untracked files, carefully.
git clean -nd
The dry run lists what would be deleted. Then git clean -fd really deletes; ignored files are only touched with -x.

Drill. From memory, in order, type: git restore file, git restore --staged file, git reset --soft HEAD~1, git reset HEAD~1, git reset --hard HEAD~1, git revert <hash>, git reflog, git stash push -m "wip", git stash pop, git clean -nd
Chapter 9. Tags and releases
When a commit matters, give it a name that never moves.
Mark the current commit as a release.
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "First release"
An annotated tag is a real object with author, date and message, which is what releases should use; git tag v1.0.0 alone makes a lightweight tag, just a name, fine for private bookmarks.
List tags.
git tag
Unlike a branch, a tag points at one commit forever.
Describe where you are relative to the last tag.
git describe --tags
v1.0.0-14-g3f2a1c9 means fourteen commits after v1.0.0 at hash 3f2a1c9. Build scripts stamp versions with it.
Delete a tag locally and on the remote.
git tag -d v1.0.0 && git push origin --delete v1.0.0
Tags are not removed by a normal push, so the remote needs its own delete.
Drill. From memory, in order, type: git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "First release", git tag, git describe --tags, git push --tags
Chapter 10. Searching and debugging
When the question is not what changed but where, or which commit broke it.
Search tracked files.
git grep -n "hello"
Respects .gitignore and is faster than grep over the tree. Add a commit at the end to search an old version without checking it out.
Follow a file across renames.
git log --follow -- hello.py
Plain log stops at a rename; --follow continues as long as the content stayed mostly the same.
Find the commit that introduced a bug by binary search.
git bisect start && git bisect bad && git bisect good v1.0.0
Git checks out the midpoint; you test and answer git bisect good or git bisect bad; the range halves each time. A thousand commits take about ten steps.
Let a test answer for you.
git bisect run make test
Git runs the command at each step and reads its exit status. git bisect reset returns you to where you started.
Check whether a file is tracked or ignored.
git ls-files | grep hello.py
ls-files lists the index. For a file that refuses to show up, git check-ignore -v path tells you which ignore rule, in which file, is hiding it.
Drill. From memory, in order, type: git grep -n "word", git log --follow -- file, git bisect start, git bisect bad, git bisect good <tag>, git bisect run make test, git bisect reset
Chapter 11. Ignoring, untracking, worktrees
Housekeeping that every real project needs.
Keep generated files out of the repository.
echo "*.log" >> .gitignore
Ignore patterns hide matching untracked files from status and add -A. They never affect files that are already tracked.
Stop tracking a file without deleting it.
git rm --cached secrets.env
The file leaves the index but stays on disk, so the ignore rule can take over. It is still in old commits; a leaked secret needs rotating, not just untracking.
Work on two branches at once in two directories.
git worktree add ../git-drill-hotfix hotfix
A second checkout attached to the same repository, no stashing or switching needed. Remove it with git worktree remove.
Embed another repository at a fixed commit.
git submodule add https://github.com/karpathy/micrograd.git vendor/micrograd
The parent records only the commit hash. A fresh clone needs git submodule update --init --recursive to fill the folder; forgetting that is why vendor folders come up empty.
Drill. From memory, in order, type: echo "*.log" >> .gitignore, git rm --cached file, git worktree add ../dir branch, git submodule update --init --recursive
Chapter 12. Under the hood
Finish by looking at the objects directly. After this, nothing git does will seem magical.
Print the commit HEAD points at.
git cat-file -p HEAD
A small text object: tree hash, parent hashes, author, committer, message. Its name is the hash of exactly this text.
Print the tree of that commit.
git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree}
Mode, type, hash and name for each entry: blobs are files, trees are directories, and a snapshot is this recursive structure, stored once per unique content.
Resolve any name to a hash.
git rev-parse HEAD
HEAD, main, v1.0.0, origin/main, HEAD~3 all become the full forty-character hash.
Hash a file's content yourself.
git hash-object README.md
The same bytes always give the same hash, in any repository anywhere. Add -w to actually store the blob.
Check the database and find orphaned objects.
git fsck
Dangling commits are often work you reset away; they can be recovered by hash.
See how much space the repository uses.
git count-objects -vH
Loose and packed object counts and sizes. git gc packs loose objects and prunes unreachable ones past the expiry window.

The whole of git follows from four ideas: content-addressed objects, trees that snapshot directories, commits that point at a tree and at parents, and refs that give commits names. Every command you typed in this book creates, moves or reads one of those.
Drill. From memory, in order, type: git cat-file -p HEAD, git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree}, git rev-parse HEAD, git hash-object README.md, git fsck, git count-objects -vH
